source: Gruenwald & Vitanyi (2008) Algorithmic Information Theory
finding: Defines K(x) as the length of the shortest program that prints x and halts, on a fixed universal language. The invariance theorem says the choice of language changes K(x) by at most an additive constant.
numbers: Invariance: K_LISP(x) <= K_Java(x) + O(1), where the constant is the size of a compiler. Attributes the idea to Solomonoff 1964, Kolmogorov 1965, Chaitin 1966.
limits: The constant can be huge for short strings, so the theory says little about any one short object. It fixes the language, not which language is natural.
agent_relevance: Shortest-rule selection (S7) is only meaningful relative to a description language. Our agent must fix one (for example a small fixed DSL) before comparing rule lengths.

source: Gruenwald & Vitanyi (2008) Algorithmic Information Theory
finding: K(x) is not computable. It is only upper semicomputable: you can find better and better upper bounds but never know when you have the best one.
numbers: No program can output K(x) for arbitrary x. Barron and Cover (1991) are quoted: you know, but you do not know you know.
quote: You know, but you do not know you know
limits: Practical use means replacing K by the output length of a real compressor, which is only an upper bound.
agent_relevance: Two candidate rules can be compared by the length of a concrete encoding, never by true K. Treat the shorter one as a tie-breaker, not as proof.

source: Gruenwald & Vitanyi (2008) Algorithmic Information Theory
finding: Links K to MDL and Occam: the best theory is the one minimising description length of theory plus data given theory. Practical MDL swaps K for probability-model codes because K is not computable.
numbers: Cites Rissanen 1978 for MDL. Two-part code: L(model)+L(data|model). Also names the algorithmic sufficient statistic and Solomonoff induction as the two ideal routes.
limits: Survey, not an experiment. Ideal MDL (K-based) and practical MDL differ.
agent_relevance: Supports the S7 tie-break 'shorter rule that fits' as a two-part code. The data-given-model term is the held-out-check pressure (G3).

source: Legg & Hutter (2007) Universal Intelligence: A Definition of Machine Intelligence
finding: Defines the universal intelligence of an agent as its expected reward over all computable environments, each weighted by 2^-K(environment). Simple environments count most.
numbers: Upsilon(pi) := sum over mu in E of 2^-K(mu) * V(mu,pi). K is defined as min{l(p): U(p)=x} on a prefix universal machine U.
limits: Not computable because K is not. Depends on the reference machine U. No empirical test; the paper surveys other tests such as the C-Test, which uses a computable proxy.
agent_relevance: A formal reason to weight simple hypotheses more. Our agent cannot compute it but can mimic it by trying short rules first.

source: Legg & Hutter (2007) Universal Intelligence
finding: Explains why simplicity is tied to compressibility: a string of a trillion zeros has a tiny program, an irregular random string has no program much shorter than itself. Cites Solomonoff induction as the sequence-prediction basis.
numbers: Example: a loop printing 0 a trillion times gives low K; a counting argument shows most strings are incompressible.
limits: Intuition only; no data.
agent_relevance: Gives the plain-language test the agent can apply: could I write a much shorter generator than the raw data?

source: Solomonoff (1964) A formal theory of inductive inference I-II
finding: [M] Founding paper of algorithmic probability: weight every program that could generate the data by 2^-length and predict by the mixture. Prediction converges fast to any computable source.
numbers: [M] Grau-Moya et al. (a22) restate the prior as M(x) = sum of 2^-l(p) over programs whose output starts with x; total prediction error is bounded by a constant set by the source's program length.
limits: Not opened this session. Needs a fixed universal machine; the constant depends on it.
agent_relevance: Origin of 'prefer shorter programs but keep all consistent ones'. A guide for weighting hypotheses in S7 without discarding alternatives.

source: Kolmogorov (1965) Three approaches to the quantitative definition of information; Chaitin (1966) On the length of programs for computing finite binary sequences
finding: [M] Independent definitions of program-length complexity (Kolmogorov 1965, Chaitin 1966), alongside Solomonoff 1964. Chaitin also proved limits on what a formal system can prove about complexity.
numbers: [M] No numbers. Dates match those given in Gruenwald & Vitanyi (a01).
limits: Not opened; only the dates were confirmed in a secondary survey.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Li, Chen, Li, Ma & Vitanyi (2004) The similarity metric (IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory)
finding: Normalized information distance (NID) built from K is a universal metric: it is below every computable normalized distance in a density-bounded class, up to small additive terms. It is not computable, so it is approximated by compressors (NCD).
numbers: NCD(x,y) = (C(xy) - min(C(x),C(y))) / max(C(x),C(y)). First applications: mitochondrial DNA phylogeny, and clustering of text and music.
limits: Optimality is for NID; NCD inherits it only if the compressor is 'normal'. Real compressors have window and block limits.
agent_relevance: A concrete computable stand-in for 'how similar are two things by shared shortest description'. Usable as a cheap dedupe or analogy-retrieval check.

source: Cilibrasi & Vitanyi (2005) Clustering by Compression
finding: NCD plus a quartet-tree method clustered 24 mammal species from raw mitochondrial genomes, with no alignment and no features. It supported the accepted (Rodents,(Primates,Ferungulates)) grouping and the Marsupionta hypothesis.
numbers: 24 species, about 17,000 bases each, PPMZ compressor, tree score S(T) = 0.996. Marsupionta favoured over Theria.
limits: Robustness shown across several compressors, but the conclusions on mammalian evolution rest on one approach compared to earlier published trees.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a crude general compressor can recover real structure. Compression tests are model-free, which fits a no-training scaffold.

source: Cilibrasi & Vitanyi (2005) Clustering by Compression
finding: Same method clustered 36 music pieces (12 pop, 12 jazz, 12 classical) from raw files. Also reported genomics, virology, languages, literature, handwritten digits and astronomy.
numbers: Music: convex clusters found with only 6 errors (three dislodged items give six misplacements). Chance probability called extremely small, but no p-value is computed.
limits: Small sample, no cross-validation, no comparison baseline for music. The chance claim is argued, not tested.
agent_relevance: Shows the style of early evidence: striking demos, not benchmarks. Later results (a12, a23) are more sobering.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) 'Low-Resource' Text Classification: A Parameter-Free Classification Method with Compressors (ACL Findings)
finding: gzip NCD plus 2-nearest-neighbour matched or beat many trained text classifiers with zero parameters. It was reported to beat BERT on all five out-of-distribution datasets and in 5-shot settings.
numbers: Test accuracy gzip vs mean of baselines: AG News .937 vs .901; DBpedia .970 vs .978; YahooAnswers .638 vs .726; 20News .685 vs .678; Ohsumed .521 vs .470; R8 .954 vs .914; R52 .896 vs .838. Beats BERT on 5 OOD sets (Kinyarwanda, Kirundi, Filipino, Swahili, Sogou).
limits: Later shown optimistic (a12): tie-breaking favoured the correct label, and the DengueFilipino test set overlaps with training. Weak on the largest set (Yahoo).
agent_relevance: The headline 'compression beats neural nets' result. A cautionary example: check evaluation leakage before trusting a compression win (G3).

source: Opitz (2023) Gzip versus bag-of-words for text classification
finding: Partial failed replication. The gzip kNN numbers used optimistic tie-breaking. With fair (random) tie-breaking gzip loses accuracy, and a plain bag-of-words distance does as well or better and is much cheaper.
numbers: Realistic accuracy drops up to 9 points versus reported. BowDist beats gzip by +1.4 points on average and wins on 6 of 7 datasets (K=2). A trained bag-of-words linear model is best overall; BERT is best with full data. DengueFilipino train and test data are identical.
limits: Single-author note; confirms gzip is still competitive in some few-shot cases, so the idea is not dead, just not special.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a compression score can look good because of evaluation artefacts. Pair any 'shorter is better' selection with an independent held-out check.

source: Soler-Toscano, Zenil, Delahaye & Gauvrit (2013) Correspondence and independence of numerical evaluations of algorithmic information measures
finding: Computes Kolmogorov-style complexity for short strings by running all small Turing machines and applying the coding theorem (output frequency implies complexity). Standard compressors fail on short strings; this method does not.
numbers: 26,559,922,791,424 machines with 5 states and 2 symbols exist; the sampled output set D(5,2) has 99,608 strings. Correlation between coding-theorem Km and number of instructions r = 0.83 (partial 0.81). Km vs Bennett logical depth r = 0.41.
limits: Reference machine is a small Turing-machine family, so values depend on that choice. Runtimes capped at 500 steps for 5-state machines.
agent_relevance: Gives a principled complexity for short rules or strings where gzip is useless. A candidate for scoring small candidate rules.

source: Gauvrit, Zenil, Delahaye & Soler-Toscano (2014) Algorithmic complexity for short binary strings applied to psychology
finding: Applies the coding-theorem complexity measure to human randomness production. Children asked to imagine 8 coin tosses produced strings more complex than a true random process gives on average, avoiding very simple strings.
numbers: N = 68 children aged 7-11 (mean 8.7). Mean complexity 21.74 (SD 0.52) vs 21.46 for random strings, t(67) = 4.35, p < 5e-5. Possible range 18.53-22.68, median 21.60. Effect of grade: F(2,65) = 0.68, not significant, eta-squared 0.11.
limits: One short-string task, small sample, no adult comparison here. Complexity measure is tied to a Turing-machine reference.
agent_relevance: Humans use complexity as a cue for 'looks random' vs 'has a rule'. Supports using low complexity as evidence of a real pattern and high complexity as evidence of noise.

source: Gauvrit et al. (2014) Algorithmic complexity for short binary strings applied to psychology
finding: Explains why entropy-based randomness scores fail for short strings and why compression-based K is unusable below about 50 symbols. Introduces the coding theorem method as the fix.
numbers: Standard Kolmogorov estimates are inapplicable for strings of length <= 50, per the abstract.
limits: Method and psychological interpretation are the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Warns that a compression-length tie-break is noisy for short rules or short traces. Prefer a symbol count in a fixed DSL.

source: Goldblum, Finzi, Rowan & Wilson (2024) The No Free Lunch Theorem, Kolmogorov Complexity, and the Role of Inductive Biases in Machine Learning
finding: Argues no-free-lunch is misleading because uniformly random data are almost all incompressible while real data are low complexity. Proves a Kolmogorov-style no-free-lunch theorem and shows language models, even randomly initialised GPT-2, prefer low-complexity sequences.
numbers: Theorem 3.1 bounds the chance of compressible labelings on uniform data. Random-init and pre-trained GPT-2 give higher probability to low-complexity bitstrings, pre-trained more so. A near-state-of-the-art vision model fits in 280 characters of PyTorch.
limits: Position paper; empirical part uses compressor-based complexity estimates on simple sequence tasks. Does not test reasoning.
agent_relevance: Justifies a built-in simplicity preference: the world is not uniform, so shorter rules are the right default. LLMs already lean this way, so the scaffold should counter it where it hurts (G3).

source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) In-Context Learning and Occam's Razor (ICML)
finding: Shows next-token loss over a context equals prequential code length, an upper bound on K(D). So training in-context learners to predict well jointly minimises training error and the complexity of the model inferred from context.
numbers: L_preq(D;T) is the area under the learner's online error curve. Experiments on regression and a Mastermind task: in-context learning infers simpler functions than gradient-based learners, but underfits in large-data regimes.
limits: Theory plus small synthetic tasks. Underfitting in large data is a stated weakness.
agent_relevance: Explains why LLM in-context rule induction already has an Occam bias, and where it fails (long contexts). The agent should add held-out checks rather than rely on it.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression (ICLR)
finding: Any predictive model plus arithmetic coding is a lossless compressor, and large text models compress images and audio better than PNG and FLAC.
numbers: Chinchilla 70B compresses ImageNet patches to 43.4% and LibriSpeech to 16.4% of raw size, vs PNG 58.5% and FLAC 30.3%. On enwik9 with 2048-byte chunks: Llama 2 7B 8.9%, Chinchilla 70B 8.3% raw, gzip 32.3%.
limits: Raw rates ignore model size. Adjusted rates (two-part code including parameters) are much worse for big models on small data; models trained on enwik8 overfit to text.
agent_relevance: Concrete measured link between prediction quality and description length. Raw vs adjusted rate is the exact trap: a short answer that hides a huge model is not simple.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression (ICLR)
finding: Reverse direction: use gzip as a generator. Sampling from a compressor works but gzip outputs are noisy, while Chinchilla completions are less noisy. In-context compression rate improves with sequence length, evidence of in-context learning.
numbers: In-context rate measured over 2048-byte subsequences averaged across 100 sequences; Chinchilla is best on all three modalities at all lengths. Larger models help only up to a critical size on a fixed dataset, after which the adjusted rate worsens.
limits: Generation quality of compressors is qualitative (images shown), no benchmark score.
agent_relevance: Scaling has a sweet spot under a two-part cost, a useful analogue for how many reasoning steps or rules to pay for.

source: Huang, Zhang, Shan & He (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly (COLM)
finding: Across 31 public LLMs and 12 benchmarks, average benchmark score is almost linear in bits per character on external text (lower BPC, higher score).
numbers: Pearson correlation about -0.93 to -0.95 across domains (knowledge and commonsense, coding, math); linear-fit RMSE 3.1% in the aggregate fit.
limits: Correlational, across models not within one; compression is measured on text matched to the tasks; benchmark scores are a proxy for intelligence; possible contamination effects.
agent_relevance: Supports compression-like measures as an unsupervised proxy for ability, but only across models. Does not show that shorter outputs in one model are more correct.

source: Grau-Moya et al. (2024) Learning Universal Predictors
finding: Trains LSTMs and Transformers on data sampled from universal Turing machines (a computable approximation of the Solomonoff prior). Larger models predict better, and UTM-trained Transformers transfer to unrelated tasks.
numbers: UTM is a BrainF-like machine (BrainPhoque). All models beat the loose Solomonoff upper bound; cumulative regret rises with the length of the generating program. Transformers transfer most to 15 Chomsky-hierarchy tasks; LSTMs to variable-order Markov sources, where large models reach near-optimal (CTW) performance.
limits: Short sequences, small UTM, computable approximation only. Shows networks can absorb universal patterns, not that they implement Solomonoff induction.
agent_relevance: Direct measured link: prediction difficulty tracks program length. Reinforces ranking hypotheses by description length.

source: Grau-Moya et al. (2024) Learning Universal Predictors
finding: Gives the formal Solomonoff prior: put uniform random bits on a monotone UTM's input tape; the output distribution is the universal prior; prediction is a mixture over all programs weighted by 2^-length.
numbers: Definition: M(x) = sum over programs p with U(p) starting with x of 2^-l(p). Convergence cost is bounded by the length of the true source's program.
limits: Incomputable without a time bound; the paper uses fixed program length and step limit.
agent_relevance: Formal template for 'weight many rules by length, do not pick one'. Useful if S7 keeps a short list of rules instead of a single one.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) The Kolmogorov Test: Compression by Code Generation (ICLR)
finding: Benchmark: give a model a data sequence at inference and ask for the shortest program that prints it. Flagship models do poorly, failing to produce a correct program on many sequences.
numbers: Llama-3.1-405B and GPT-4o fail to output a correct program for 78% and 40% of natural-data sequences, and 66% and 45% of synthetic ones (introduction; Section 5.1 says over 65% and 55% for synthetic). Data: audio (8-bit, MFCC), text, DNA, synthetic. Precision (compression vs gzip ratio) above 1.0 means worse than gzip.
limits: The paper's two statements of synthetic failure rates differ slightly. The metric uses a compression ratio against gzip, which depends on gzip behaviour at short length.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of shortest-program search: even large models often fail. The agent should not expect to find the shortest rule unaided; add a verification step.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) The Kolmogorov Test
finding: Training small code models (SeqCoder) on synthetic program-sequence pairs beats prompted frontier models on synthetic data and is the only approach to beat gzip there, but gains barely transfer to real data.
numbers: SeqCoder reaches about 84.5% to 92.5% accuracy on the synthetic distribution with precision below 1.0 (0.57, 0.56), but near zero on natural audio, DNA and text. Over 99% of failed SeqCoder programs have an error in the first 16 characters.
limits: Accuracy numbers read from a table whose columns I matched by position. The synthetic distribution is the authors' own DSL, so in-distribution.
agent_relevance: Shows overfitting to a prior: good at short programs in the training language, useless outside it. A warning for any learned simplicity prior.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) The Kolmogorov Test
finding: Error analysis: models compress mainly by copying (repetitions explain most correct natural-data programs but few synthetic ones), and make over-simplified programs that miss the sequence or over-complicated ones that work.
numbers: Repetition accounts for more than 95% of correct programs on natural data on average, 20% on synthetic. In over 30% of cases models split the sequence into sub-sequences then merge with small errors. A uniform prior over the DSL gives modest gains; inline execution feedback adds modest gains.
limits: Manual analysis of 25 errors per condition, so counts are rough.
agent_relevance: Two failure types to guard against in S7: too-short rules that do not fit the data, and bloated rules that fit. Execution feedback helps only a little, so check against held-out cases.

source: Li & Vitanyi (1997) An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Applications
finding: [M] Standard textbook: invariance, incompressibility counting argument, prefix complexity, Solomonoff-Levin universal distribution, coding theorem (K(x) = -log m(x) + O(1)), MDL.
numbers: [M] Counting argument: fewer than 2^n programs shorter than n bits, so most n-bit strings are incompressible.
limits: Not opened; cited repeatedly by opened papers (a01, a08, a09).
agent_relevance: Background for the claim that most data are noise and short descriptions are rare, so finding one is real evidence.

source: Gruenwald & Vitanyi (2008) Algorithmic Information Theory
finding: Explains the compression approximation: use an existing data compressor to obtain a computable upper bound on K, accepting that this loses the optimality guarantee.
numbers: Text states K can be approximated after all, in a weaker sense, by taking an existing data compression program.
limits: No claim is made about how close real compressors get to K.
agent_relevance: Licence to use concrete measures (token count, compressed size) as proxies for rule length.

source: Gauvrit et al. (2014) Algorithmic complexity for short binary strings applied to psychology
finding: Positions K as the one measure that unifies the separate randomness scores (entropy, runs, symmetry) used in psychology; notes that symmetry, complementation and repetition are recognised by the new measure.
numbers: Text states symmetry, complementation and repetition are on average recognised by D(5).
limits: Interpretive claim by the authors; no meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Bridge to cognitive science: what humans call a pattern lines up with what has a short program.

source: Gruenwald & Vitanyi (2008), covering Shannon entropy and MDL background (Cover & Thomas 1991; Rissanen 1978)
finding: The survey notes Shannon entropy bounds average code length (noiseless coding theorem), while K deals with single objects. MDL (Rissanen 1978) is the practical statistical form.
numbers: Noiseless coding theorem: optimal average code length equals entropy. K concerns individual sequences, entropy concerns distributions.
limits: Cross-reference only; Shannon and MDL are other subfields (01, 03).
agent_relevance: Link to sibling subfields; avoid duplicating their content.
